name: Lateral elbow tendinopathy

diagnosisContested.note: The clinical diagnosis is established, and history and physical examination are described as the gold standard. The underlying mechanism is less settled: the JOSPT guideline describes an interplay of tendon changes, motor control impairment and possible changes in pain processing. Several conditions can mimic it, including cervical radiculopathy, radial tunnel syndrome and posterior interosseous syndrome, so a self-reported label may be wrong.

avoidOrModify.movement: Loaded wrist extensor work at a load that aggravates symptoms
avoidOrModify.rationale: The guideline says applied loads should not exacerbate symptoms, and that loading should progress from isometric to isotonic to eccentric as tolerated. It also notes that no study described how load was determined or progressed, so this rule rests largely on expert opinion.

avoidOrModify.movement: Repeated wrist or elbow flexion and extension that aggravates symptoms, especially for long periods
avoidOrModify.rationale: Repetitive elbow or wrist flexion and extension for more than 2 hours a day is listed as a modifiable risk factor, and the guideline says aggravating repetitive motions should be minimized. This comes from risk-factor data and guideline narrative, not from trials showing that reducing these motions improves outcomes.

avoidOrModify.movement: Repeated forearm twisting, rotating or screwing motions
avoidOrModify.rationale: Listed by the guideline as a modifiable risk factor. Risk-factor association only, with no trial showing that reducing it helps.

avoidOrModify.movement: Lifting objects with the forearm pronated (palm facing down)
avoidOrModify.rationale: The guideline says this should be minimized, in a narrative statement under ergonomics. Its ergonomics recommendation is grade E, and very little evidence is specific to this condition. Applying it to palm-down gym lifts such as reverse curls is an extrapolation made for this app.

avoidOrModify.movement: Handling very heavy loads in the hands
avoidOrModify.rationale: Handling heavy tools over 20 kg is listed as a modifiable risk factor. This is occupational data. Applying it to loaded carries or heavy barbell work is an extrapolation made for this app, and the 20 kg figure should not be treated as a gym threshold.

candidateExercises.name: Wrist extension with a light dumbbell

dose.frequency: Guideline suggests 3 sets of 15 for 6-12 weeks, without stating a weekly frequency. Trial programs were often daily, but frequency and load varied.

candidateExercises.cautions: Load should not exacerbate symptoms. The best dose and load are unknown, and no study described how load was determined or progressed. Benefits are small. Not advised as a progression until an isometric version is tolerated, under the guideline's expert-opinion sequence.

candidateExercises.name: Isometric wrist extension hold

dose.frequency: Guideline's general suggestion is 3 sets of 15 for 6-12 weeks, and it applies this to isometric work too. The isometric trial used a daily program for 8 weeks. Its hold time, sets and reps were not available in the sources opened, so hold time is left empty.

candidateExercises.cautions: Do not invent a hold time. The trial used a container of water with a handle as resistance, so this is not a true no-equipment exercise. It improved disability and worst pain versus wait-and-see, but not global improvement or pain-free grip strength, and its authors question it as a sole treatment.

candidateExercises.name: Eccentric wrist extension with a rubber bar

dose.frequency: Daily for 7 weeks in the Tyler 2010 trial, as tabulated by Yoon 2021.

candidateExercises.cautions: Requires a rubber bar, and the exact technique was not verified in the sources opened. Evidence is limited: 6 trials with risk-of-bias concerns and varied protocols. Compared with concentric or isotonic exercise the pain benefit was small, with no clear difference in strength or function. Progress only as tolerated without exacerbating symptoms.

candidateExercises.name: Shoulder and scapular stabilizer training

dose.frequency: Not established in the sources opened.

candidateExercises.cautions: Grade C, only when impairments have been identified, and alongside wrist extensor strengthening. An app cannot identify those impairments, and the guideline passage reviewed names no specific exercises, so this does not justify mapping to a catalog exercise. The trials conflict: Mostafaee 2020 favored adding it, while Day 2021 found no added value in a multimodal program.

redFlags.sign: Atypical mass or swelling around the elbow
redFlags.action: Stop elbow-loading exercise and seek urgent medical assessment.
Stop elbow-loading exercise and seek urgent medical assessment.
Stop elbow-loading exercise and seek urgent medical assessment.

redFlags.sign: Feeling systemically unwell, malaise or weight loss alongside elbow symptoms
redFlags.action: Stop elbow-loading exercise and seek urgent medical assessment.

redFlags.sign: Progressive weakness when extending the fingers or wrist
redFlags.action: Stop loading the arm and get prompt medical assessment. This can point to posterior interosseous nerve compression. The source sets no timing, so 'prompt' is this report's wording.

redFlags.sign: Symptoms that may come from another condition, such as the neck or a nerve entrapment, or that do not fit the usual pattern
redFlags.action: Get a professional evaluation. The guideline says therapists should identify conditions that mimic this one and promptly refer when appropriate. It lists the conditions but not patient-facing signs, so the wording here is this report's own.

limitations: Overall grade is low. Karanasios 2021 rates its evidence low to very low certainty and finds small effects. The guideline gives exercise grade B, but states that its 3 x 15 for 6-12 weeks dose comes from best available evidence and expert opinion, that no study described load determination or progression, and that the best exercise type and dose remain unknown. Trial protocols varied widely. The guideline covers literature published before November 2021, and no later systematic review was read. Coverage gaps: the NICE CKS page and the BESS tennis elbow pathway (Singh 2023, DOI 10.1177/17585732231170793) could not be opened, so neither is cited; no Cochrane review was opened. Karanasios 2021 and Vuvan 2020 were read as abstracts only, and the Tyler 2010 protocol only as tabulated in Yoon 2021. Red flags come from one local NHS pathway and one case-based article, not from a validated screening tool, and patient-facing wording is partly this report's own. Applying occupational risk factors to gym movements is an extrapolation. This is general information and not treatment or diagnosis.

itemsRemoved.item: avoidOrModify: Hard or sustained gripping that provokes lateral elbow pain, such as hangs or heavy carries
itemsRemoved.reason: No cited source supports it. The guideline mentions gripping only as a provoking test in a trial's inclusion criteria, and NHS Tayside says only 'Modify loading' and gives no gripping advice. The item's own text called it an inference. nhs_tayside was then unused and was removed.

No source recommends it as a candidate or gives a dose. The guideline's exercise recommendation covers resisted exercise only, and the trials it describes tested stretching only combined with strengthening, so no source isolates a benefit from stretching.

unverifiable: The publisher copy of Lucado 2022 returned 403. The full text was read from the orthopt.org PDF, which carries the JOSPT download stamp.
Red flags: 'Stop elbow-loading exercise' is not in the NHS Highland pathway. Its clinician-facing action is an urgent call to on-call orthopaedics plus a referral.
Cha 2014 names progressive weakness of the digit extensors and extensor carpi radialis brevis. 'Wrist' is an anatomical reading of that muscle, not the article's word.
The Tyler 2010 protocol was checked only as tabulated in Yoon 2021. Vuvan 2020 hold time, sets and reps were not checked in its full text.
